opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, autonomy is really the dividing line between a tool and an agent.

Most of what we've built with large models so far is still fundamentally reactive. You give it a prompt, it gives you an answer, and the loop closes. Even when we chain tools together, a human is usually designing the workflow and deciding what happens next. That's useful, but it's closer to a very smart function call than to an agent.

An agent, in the sense I care about, should be able to take a goal that's somewhat underspecified, break it down on its own, decide what information it needs, act in an environment, look at the feedback, and adjust, over a long horizon and without someone holding its hand at every step. That ability to self-direct is what autonomy means to me. Without it, you don't really get the compounding value. The value of an agent comes from the fact that it can run for hours or days and make many decisions you never had to think about.

There's also a deeper, more research-oriented reason. If you look at how intelligence develops, in humans or in reinforcement learning systems, a lot of it comes from interacting with the world and learning from consequences, not just imitating data. Pretraining on human text gives you an enormous prior, but it's essentially learning from what others have already done. To go beyond that, the system has to explore, try things, fail, and figure out what works. That requires autonomy almost by definition. So I see autonomy not only as a product feature but as a path toward models that can keep improving from their own experience.

Of course, autonomy brings real challenges. Long-horizon reliability is hard: small errors accumulate. Evaluation is hard, because the tasks are open-ended. And safety and controllability become much more important when the system is making its own decisions. So I don't think of autonomy as "remove the human entirely." It's more about shifting the human's role from micromanaging each step to setting goals, defining boundaries, and checking outcomes. Getting that balance right is, I think, one of the central problems of the next few years.

fable-5.1.text:
Autonomy is central because, honestly, without it the word "agent" doesn't mean much. If a system only acts when you push it, step by step, then it's a tool. A very good tool, maybe, but the intelligence is still sitting on your side of the screen. What makes something an agent is that it can carry an intention forward on its own: it decides what to look at next, it notices when the plan isn't working, it goes back and tries something else, and it does all that without you babysitting every move.

I think of it a bit like the difference between a calculator and a colleague. A calculator is perfectly accurate, but every single step is mine. A colleague takes a goal and comes back with something. They've made dozens of small decisions along the way that I never had to think about. That is where the real value is. The economic and practical leverage comes precisely from the decisions you don't have to make yourself.

There's also a deeper reason, which is about how capability actually develops. If you constrain a system to only execute predetermined steps, you're capping it at the level of whoever wrote the steps. Autonomy is what lets the system exceed its instructions, explore, hit dead ends, and learn from them. In our own work we've seen this clearly: the moment you give a model a longer leash, a real environment, and the ability to run many steps before anyone checks in, it starts solving things that simply weren't reachable in a single-turn setting. The gains didn't come from a smarter one-shot answer. They came from the loop.

Of course, autonomy brings its own problems. More freedom means more ways to go wrong, and you have to think hard about verification, about when the system should stop and ask, about keeping humans in a position to understand what happened. But I'd frame those as the engineering challenges of agents, not reasons to avoid autonomy. If you take autonomy out to make the problems disappear, you've also taken out the thing that made it worth building.

astra-6.text:
To me, autonomy is what makes an AI system an agent. It’s not just answering a question; it’s taking a goal, deciding what to do next, acting, and adjusting based on what happens. If a person has to specify every step, the person is still doing most of that work.

But autonomy doesn’t mean unlimited freedom. A useful agent needs to understand the boundaries of its task, recognize when it lacks information, and know when to ask for help. The point is to let people delegate meaningful work while retaining control over the decisions that matter.

sol-6.1.text:
I see autonomy as central because an agent needs to do more than respond to a single instruction. It needs to take a goal, decide what to do next, act, and use the results to adjust its plan. If a human has to direct every step, much of that work still falls on the human.

But autonomy doesn’t mean unlimited freedom. A useful agent should operate within clear boundaries, recognize when it lacks information, and ask for help when a decision exceeds its authority. The point is to let it carry meaningful work forward while keeping the human in control of the goal and the constraints.
